---
name: plan-from-spec
description: Turns planning/spec.md into planning/plan.md before any code is written - ordered build steps, each naming the spec lines it meets and the test written first, with the test plan inside the plan. Use when asked to plan the build from the spec, or to write or fix the test plan.
---

# Plan from the spec

Write `planning/plan.md` from `planning/spec.md`. Write no application code and no tests in this
step: the plan is read and corrected by a person before anything is built.

## Read first

- `planning/spec.md`: the numbered requirements (R-01, R-02, ...) and how each is checked.
- `CHALLENGE.md`, `docs/requirements.md`, `materials/office-policy.md` and `snapshot.schema.json`:
  the sources the spec was written from.
- The request exports in `materials/requests/`: open the ones a test case uses, and read their
  `message` text.

## Write `planning/plan.md` with these four sections

1. **Choices.** The runtime, the interface (a CLI, a service or a web application), the test
   command, and how the model provider is called. One line each, with its reason.
2. **Steps, in build order.** A numbered list. Each step names the spec lines it meets
   (`R-03, R-07`), the test from the test plan that is written first and seen to fail, and what is
   true when the step is done. The first step builds the mock provider the tests use. Each test
   belongs to one step only, so every step has a test that fails until that step's code exists.
3. **Test plan.** A table, one row per case:

   | Case | Input | Mock response | Expected facts | Source of the expected facts | Spec lines |
   |---|---|---|---|---|---|

   - One row for each case in `docs/requirements.md` § Verification: a complete request, missing
     dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun and
     changed source content; then the paraphrased synthetic request, a refusal or interrupted
     response, and a failed retry after a prior success.
   - **Input** names the export file (or the new message you author) that shows the case. Find it by
     reading the messages.
   - **Mock response** says what the mock provider returns for that case: a reply saved under
     `tests/mock_responses/`, an error, or a cut-off reply. No test calls the real provider.
   - **Expected facts** are the field values, status, owner and next action the case must produce.
     Write them from the message text and the office policy, never from running the code.
   - **Source of the expected facts** quotes the words of the message and the policy rule they
     come from.
4. **Coverage.** Every spec line, each with the step that builds it and the test or check that
   shows it. A spec line with no step or no test is listed under "Not yet covered", with the reason.

## Before you finish

- Every spec line appears in § Coverage with a step and a test, or under "Not yet covered".
- Every expected fact has a quote from a message or the policy beside it.
- Every case of § Verification has its own row.
- No step and no test needs `API_KEY`.
- No test is named by two steps.

Where a spec line is unclear, say so in the plan and ask the person; do not guess a rule.
Entire's CLI is the source of truth for its own usage. Do not guess flags or
subcommands — read them from this command. You are already inside the repo:
entire auto-detects it from the git origin remote, so never ask the user for the
repo name. Pass --repo only to target a DIFFERENT repo.
Trails are project-scoped. Trail listing requires an explicit --project (--repo only filters within it), or --mine for your trails across projects.

Current repo: gh/MyWorkTraining/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests  (auto-detected from origin; pass --repo only for a DIFFERENT repo)

When to use entire — the commands that bear on the work:
  checkpoint  Inspect and search checkpoints
                read-only except: delete, explain, push
  search      Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using semantic and keyword matching
                read-only
  session     Manage agent sessions tracked by Entire
                read-only except: adopt, attach, resume, stop
  status      Show Entire status
                read-only
  trail       Manage trails across repositories and branches
                read-only: approvals, list, sessions, show, stack, timeline, watch — others write
  why         Show why a line exists
                read-only

Also available (entire agent-help <command> for any of these):
  read-only, safe to run:
    activity · labs · recap · version
  when the task needs them:
    api · dispatch · doctor
  the user's — suggest, don't run:
    agent · auth · clean · cluster · configure · disable · enable
    login · logout · org · plugin · project · repo · service-account

Drill in for exact, currently-installed flags:  entire agent-help <command>  (e.g. entire agent-help checkpoint)
Add --json for structured output.

# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.
# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

# Northstar access-request intake

A Python CLI turns exported free-text messages into schema-validated extraction records and an ordered human-review queue. It prepares requests for people; a named manager is a contact, and successful intake never means approval.

## Setup and tests

Supported environment: Python 3.11+ on a local POSIX filesystem; this submission was exercised with Python 3.12 on Linux. Install `uv`, then run from the repository root:

```bash
uv sync --frozen
. .venv/bin/activate
env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

`pyproject.toml` declares jsonschema; `uv.lock` locks it and its dependencies. Setup may download locked packages. Tests and mock intake need no credentials or network. The tests forbid sockets and any read of API_KEY, including in guarded CLI subprocesses. A real-provider authentication unit check injects an inert credential function and inspects the environment-reader source; it never calls that reader. Target one planned test with `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -k test_r53_contract -v`; zero discovered tests is not a pass.

## Reproducible mock intake and inspection

These commands run after activation from the repository root. Use a fresh database path for a fresh demonstration; rerunning the same input/configuration reuses completed valid work.

<!-- smoke -->
```bash
python3 -m intake run --input materials/requests --db var/demo.sqlite --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses --output deliverables
python3 -m intake queue --db var/demo.sqlite --include-pending
python3 -m intake resume --db var/demo.sqlite --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses
python3 -m intake retry --db var/demo.sqlite --document IT-010.json --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses
python3 -m intake history --db var/demo.sqlite --document IT-010.json
python3 -m intake export --db var/demo.sqlite --output deliverables
```

`run` accepts a directory or one exported JSON file. `queue` reads committed current outcomes even while another CLI process is preparing other documents; `--include-pending` also shows pending/running work without pretending it has a completed business status. `history` retains every attempt with its source bytes/hash, configuration, policy identity and outcome. Inputs absent from a later batch remain present. A corrected message or relevant producing-settings change creates a new attempt; `--refresh` explicitly forces one. Explicit retry bypasses reuse, and a failed retry becomes the current error while previous success remains identifiable in history.

Run recovery with `resume` after a crash or deployment interruption. It continues pending work and running work whose claim expired; the default claim lifetime is request timeout + 5 seconds. An active claim is left alone. Resume reconstructs settings per document, supports parallel progress and refreshes work if prompt/schema/policy versions changed. An older or expired worker token cannot replace a newer claim's result. Pending work with changed settings is marked superseded in history rather than mislabelled as produced under those earlier settings.

Each error includes an actionable diagnostic and a reproducible `retry_command`; use that command against the same recorded database/configuration. CLI exit status is 0 on successful execution, 1 when current error records or failed accuracy comparisons remain, and 2 for command/input/configuration errors. A `needs-information` request is successful intake awaiting clarification, not an extraction error.

## Keyboard and screen-reader operation

Add `--format text` after any subcommand for labelled output in reading order. This mode uses ordinary terminal text with no color, animation, cursor control or timed input. Each queue entry starts with its document name and work state, followed by its routing, errors and retry guidance when available. In history, each attempt has its own state, source and producing settings. Use the terminal's screen-reader navigation commands to review earlier lines. Font size, contrast and cursor preferences are set in the terminal.

```bash
python3 -m intake --help
python3 -m intake queue --help
python3 -m intake queue --db var/demo.sqlite --include-pending --format text
python3 -m intake history --db var/demo.sqlite --document IT-010.json --format text
```

Use the same `--format text` option with `run`, `resume`, `retry`, `export` and `accuracy`. While intake or resume is active, inspect progress from a second terminal with `queue --include-pending`. Read the `Retry command` line under the failed document and run it to retry that document. `export --format text` identifies the published generation, and `accuracy --format text` gives the match count and report path. JSON remains the default for command output and the format of the machine-readable exports.

Use a keyboard-operable terminal exposing its text through the platform's accessibility services, such as Xfce Terminal with Orca on Linux. See the [Section 508 verification results](deliverables/verification.md#section-508-accessibility) for tested versions, workflows and pending checks.

## Provider configuration

Mock mode reads only saved JSON replies and the development manifest under `tests/mock_responses/`; it never reads API_KEY. `--script` selects another saved manifest. Reply sequences reset when a new mock process is created; the durable record of attempts remains in SQLite. The production extractor does not look up known filenames or import tests/expected. `--mock-gates` is a development-only directory of file barriers for repeatable process/interruption tests.

Implemented live configuration: OpenAI Responses API, explicit `--model` (the documented reference configuration is `gpt-4.1-mini`), HTTPS endpoint `https://api.openai.com/v1/responses`, structured JSON schema with strict mode, `store=false`, and `--max-output-tokens 4096`. The prompt is `intake/prompt.txt`, and the schema is `snapshot.schema.json`. The adapter validates completed responses, refusal content, malformed JSON, schema types and literal evidence before routing. It does not execute embedded source instructions.

For an optional live run, have the operator supply API_KEY through the environment and select `--provider openai --model gpt-4.1-mini`. This implementation session did not read a real key, call a real model, or observe live performance. `API_KEY` is the only application credential environment variable. Model/provider/endpoint/timeouts are CLI configuration, not inferred from environment variables; changing `--endpoint` requires a compatible HTTPS service. Authentication is loaded lazily only by the real adapter. Logs/errors/evidence omit credential values and untrusted provider error bodies.

`run`, `resume` and `retry` accept `--workers` (default 4), `--timeout` seconds (default 30), `--max-retries` (default 0) and `--retry-delay` seconds (default 1, exponential between retryable attempts). Retries are bounded per document. Request limits, temporary provider errors and timeouts affect the document involved while other workers can continue. There is no organization-wide quota coordinator. Request settings, prompt/schema hashes and policy hash are persisted; changes to relevant production/routing settings refresh affected results. Policy changes currently re-extract rather than optimize to rerouting alone.

Provider request and response fields were checked against the official [Responses reference](https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/responses/methods/create), [structured outputs guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/structured-outputs) and [model documentation](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-4.1-mini). `deliverables/request-evidence.json` is an intercepted real-adapter request backed by a saved mock reply, with credential redaction; it is not a live observation.

## Accuracy and source evidence

```bash
python3 -m intake accuracy --input materials/requests --synthetic tests/fixtures/IT-P01.json --expected tests/expected --responses tests/mock_responses --provider mock --output deliverables/accuracy.md
```

Expected facts were authored from the plan/messages/policy before extraction runs, separately from the mocked provider replies. The synthetic input uses filename IT-P01.json to match its stated identifier and preserve the plan's complete staging/read case. The report contains 20 supplied cases plus that paraphrase, exact source quotes, producing configuration and 11 non-purpose scalar comparisons per case (231 total). Missing/error or duplicate-case extraction counts as 11 mismatches; nulls count and comparisons are exact, case-sensitive, without normalization. Extra cases, routing errors and schema/evidence/issues problems are reported separately. Purpose prose is reviewed against source evidence separately; a faithful paraphrase is not rejected for differing wording. Nonliteral purpose output is flagged for manual semantic review rather than automatically declared factually wrong. The JSON findings are saved beside the Markdown report.

The mock result tests the pipeline, not live model accuracy. It cannot establish fresh-wording extraction quality or universal resistance to instruction attacks. Factual-error mutation tests deliberately change otherwise valid saved-response facts so copied or self-derived expectations cannot silently pass. No minimum accuracy score or latency/throughput threshold has been invented.

## Shared operation, history and publication limits

Support is for multiple CLI processes on one host sharing one local SQLite database and local output directory; multi-host and network-share locking are not supported. Transactions keep claims/current pointers coherent. Immutable attempts are separate from current outputs. The latest accepted ingestion order controls the current source revision; export timestamps are display metadata. A late response can be retained in earlier history but cannot replace a newer current document revision.

Exports are generated from one committed snapshot. An advisory publisher lock serializes snapshot-to-publication work. `deliverables/current` atomically selects an immutable `.generations/` directory, and `extractions.jsonl`/`queue.json` are stable links through it. A reader inspecting both files during concurrent publication must resolve and pin `current` once, then read both files in that directory. Abandoned unpublished generations may remain on disk after interruption; retain them for investigation. Export again to publish the latest database state. The database is authoritative between exports.

The source's ordinary 200–400 messages/day and roughly 2,000-message bursts are operating context, not measured capacity. Verification covers the 20 supplied messages, a paraphrase, controlled concurrency/failure/interruption scenarios, and a 200-word input. It includes no 2,000-message load test, distributed deployment check, power-loss durability certification, live quota test or live-model accuracy measurement. Generic free-text facts and attack intent still need human scrutiny; exact quotes and schema checks cannot prove all semantics.

See `deliverables/verification.md` for per-step red/green evidence, assertions and remaining external checks. Final facilitator session-capture pairing and Classroom submission are external acceptance work; the application and the mock suite do not perform them.

# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

All provider observations here use saved mock responses or intercepted transport, with no live model call. The scalar result is pipeline validation, not live model accuracy. Expected facts come from planning/plan.md and exact message/policy evidence in tests/expected; the mock provider never reads that oracle.

## Commands and comparisons

Run after `uv sync --frozen` and activation from the repository root:

```bash
env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -k Step11 -v
python3 -m intake run --input materials/requests --db var/verification.sqlite --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses --output deliverables
```

## Operating assumptions and limits

Supported arrangement: concurrent CLI processes on one host using local SQLite and POSIX advisory file locks, symlinks, rename and fsync; multi-host/shared network filesystems are not supported or verified. Current reads are transactional database views; static files are point-in-time snapshots and readers must pin one generation across multi-file inspection. Default concurrency is four requests, request timeout is 30 seconds and claim lifetime is timeout plus 5 seconds. Retryable failures have configurable bounded exponential retries, default zero; there is no shared organization-wide request-rate coordinator.

The brief's 200–400 ordinary daily messages and roughly 2,000-message burst are context. No 2,000-message load test, throughput/latency SLA, distributed recovery or actual power-loss test was performed. Process termination, fake clock expiry, thread/process barriers and publication fault hooks exercise specific recovery paths; they do not simulate every filesystem/hardware outage. Mock fixture sequences reset per mock process, and fixtures intentionally contain known facts. """Plan-owned contracts: disk response fixtures, no network or credential reads."""
import importlib
import importlib.util
import os
from pathlib import Path
import socket
import unittest
from unittest import mock

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
MOCKS = ROOT / 'tests' / 'mock_responses'


class Contract(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.addCleanup(mock.patch.stopall)
        mock.patch.object(socket, 'socket', side_effect=AssertionError('network forbidden')).start()
        original_getitem = os._Environ.__getitem__

        def guarded_getitem(environment, key):
            if key == 'API_KEY':
                raise AssertionError('tests must not read API_KEY')
            return original_getitem(environment, key)

        mock.patch.object(os._Environ, '__getitem__', guarded_getitem).start()

    def providers(self):
        self.assertIsNotNone(
            importlib.util.find_spec('intake.providers'),
            'Step 1 mock provider behavior has not been implemented',
        )
        return importlib.import_module('intake.providers')

    def module(self, name):
        self.assertIsNotNone(importlib.util.find_spec(name), f'{name} behavior has not been implemented')
        return importlib.import_module(name)

    def reply(self, name):
        import json
        return json.loads((MOCKS / name).read_text())

    def document(self, number=1):
        return self.module('intake.source').load(ROOT / f'materials/requests/IT-{number:03d}.json')

    def expected(self, name='IT-001.json'):
        import json
        return json.loads((ROOT / 'tests/expected' / name).read_text())


class Step01(Contract):
    def test_mock_provider_contract(self):
        """TP-01: ordered saved success/error responses and explicit unscripted errors."""
        providers = self.providers()
        provider = providers.MockProvider(
            MOCKS,
            {'one.json': ['provider-complete.json', 'provider-error.json']},
        )
        self.assertEqual(provider.complete({'document_id': 'one.json'})['status'], 'completed')
        with self.assertRaisesRegex(providers.ProviderError, 'temporarily unavailable'):
            provider.complete({'document_id': 'one.json'})
        self.assertEqual(provider.calls, ['one.json', 'one.json'])
        with self.assertRaisesRegex(providers.ProviderError, 'unscripted'):
            provider.complete({'document_id': 'unknown.json'})

    def test_mock_transport_contract(self):
        """TP-01: saved refusal/interruption responses and exact request recording."""
        providers = self.providers()
        transport = providers.MockTransport(
            MOCKS, ['provider-refusal.json', 'provider-interrupted.json'],
        )
        refusal = transport({'model': 'fixture-model'})
        self.assertEqual(refusal['status'], 'completed')
        self.assertEqual(refusal['output'][0]['content'][0]['type'], 'refusal')
        self.assertEqual(transport({'model': 'fixture-model'})['status'], 'incomplete')
        self.assertEqual(transport.requests, [{'model': 'fixture-model'}, {'model': 'fixture-model'}])


class Step02(Contract):
    def test_r03_contract(self):
        import json
        import tempfile
        source = self.module('intake.source')
        for path in sorted((ROOT / 'materials/requests').glob('*.json')):
            self.assertIsInstance(source.load(path)['message'], str)
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
            path = Path(directory) / 'fresh.json'
            path.write_text(json.dumps({'message': ' '.join(['word'] * 200)}))
            self.assertEqual(len(source.load(path)['message'].split()), 200)

    def test_r04_contract(self):

**Accessibility replay.** For each TP-52 run, use a fresh temporary database, input directory, output directory and gate directory. Start `run` with `--provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses`, the temporary initial manifest via `--script`, the gate directory via `--mock-gates` and at least three workers. Use a timeout long enough for manual inspection. Wait for the `entered` marker and use `queue --include-pending` in a second terminal until IT-001 is unfinished, IT-002 reads `Security Review / review / review-risk-then-owner`, and IT-010 reads `IT Service Desk / error / retry-extraction`. Interrupt the first invocation while IT-001 is blocked, let its claim expire, create the `release` marker, and resume against the same database and gates. IT-001 then reads `System Owner / review / review-request` and IT-002 keeps its original result. For the displayed IT-010 retry command, use the completed mock manifest and expect `IT Service Desk / needs-information / clarify` because its end date remains missing. Verify that history retains the failed attempt and that export, evidence and reports are available with equivalent information. Run each CLI command with `API_KEY` unset and record the commands and mock setup for replay. For TP-54 automation, reuse the guarded subprocess runner and deterministic claim expiry used by TP-46.

**Test ownership and commands.** TP-01’s two named support tests belong only to step 1. All spec-named automated tests have their single owner in Coverage. For manual acceptance rows, add these distinct step-owned smoke tests without replacing the human check: step 10 owns `test_accuracy_arithmetic` and `test_accuracy_report_contract` (TP-49); step 11 owns `test_readme_command_smoke` and `test_package_manifest_contract` (TP-51). `test_r70_contract` owns the independent-oracle mutation check (TP-48). The named filter must discover at least one test. Step 4 exclusively owns `test_provider_transport_outcomes`, which unit-checks provider error/refusal/completion normalization before the step-7 persisted-error acceptance tests. Support/smoke tests use the same command with their own method name. No test may call the real provider; intercepted transport tests cover the actual adapter code path.

**Limits and unresolved source terms.** The sources supply no numerical workload SLA, minimum accuracy percentage, exact prose normalization or full attack-detection algorithm. This plan does not supply new business rules for those gaps. Implement and test the supplied override case, document other detection assumptions and state that mocked attacks do not establish universal resistance. The planned field-counting convention is disclosed separately from factual correctness; a semantically faithful purpose summary must not fail solely because it differs from a canned sentence. Configuration identities, claim lifetimes, retry limits and concurrency are implementation settings whose chosen values and measured limits must be documented. Model IDs and actual response envelopes must be verified against official provider documentation during step 4; no unsupported live-result claim is permitted. None of these choices requires a facilitator key or a live call to finish the planned mock checks.

def add_output_format(command):
    command.add_argument('--format', choices=('json', 'text'), default='json',
                         help='Choose JSON or labelled plain text (default: JSON).')


def parser():
    result = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='Process access requests and inspect the human-review queue.')
    commands = result.add_subparsers(dest='command', required=True)
    descriptions = {
        'run': 'Start intake for one export or a directory of exports.',
        'queue': 'Read the current review queue.',
        'resume': 'Continue recorded unfinished work.',
        'retry': 'Run a new attempt for one document.',
        'history': 'Read previous attempts and their source and settings.',
        'export': 'Publish the current queue and extraction files.',
    }
    for command, description in descriptions.items():
        sub = commands.add_parser(command, help=description, description=description)
        sub.add_argument('--db', default='var/intake.sqlite')
        add_output_format(sub)
        if command in ('run', 'resume', 'retry'):
            sub.add_argument('--provider', choices=['mock', 'openai'])
            sub.add_argument('--responses')
            sub.add_argument('--script')
            sub.add_argument('--mock-gates')
            sub.add_argument('--model')
            sub.add_argument('--endpoint')
            sub.add_argument('--timeout', type=float)
            sub.add_argument('--max-output-tokens', type=int)
            sub.add_argument('--workers', type=int, default=4)
            sub.add_argument('--max-retries', type=int, default=0)
            sub.add_argument('--retry-delay', type=float, default=1)
            sub.add_argument('--output')
        if command == 'run':
            sub.add_argument('--input', required=True)
            sub.add_argument('--refresh', action='store_true')
        if command in ('history', 'retry'):
            sub.add_argument('--document', required=True, help='Input filename, including .json.')
        if command == 'queue':
            sub.add_argument('--include-pending', action='store_true', help='Include recorded unfinished work.')
        if command == 'export':
            sub.add_argument('--output', required=True)
    accuracy = commands.add_parser('accuracy', help='Compare mock or provider results with source expectations.')
    add_output_format(accuracy)
    accuracy.add_argument('--input', required=True)
    accuracy.add_argument('--synthetic')
    accuracy.add_argument('--expected', required=True)
    accuracy.add_argument('--responses', default='tests/mock_responses')
    accuracy.add_argument('--provider', choices=['mock', 'openai'], default='mock')
    accuracy.add_argument('--model')
    accuracy.add_argument('--output', required=True)
    return result


def make_runner(args, store, prior_override=None):
    prior = {}
    if args.command == 'retry':
        history = store.history(args.document)
        if history:
            prior = history[-1]['settings']
    elif args.command == 'resume' and store.pending():
        prior = store.pending()[0]['settings']
    if prior_override is not None:
        prior = prior_override

# Build plan for the IT access-request intake

This plan maps all 114 [specification requirements](spec.md) to build steps and acceptance checks. The [implementation and acceptance record](#implementation-and-acceptance-record) gives the status of the build, Section 508 checks, and final submission.

## Choices

- **Runtime:** Python 3.11 or later, standard-library `unittest`, `sqlite3`, `argparse`, hashing and HTTP transport, with `jsonschema` declared in `pyproject.toml` and dependencies locked in `uv.lock`; this fits the supplied Python test harness and keeps deployment small.
- **Interface:** a CLI invoked as `python3 -m intake`, with `run`, `queue`, `resume`, `retry`, `history`, `export` and `accuracy` subcommands; separate invocations can inspect committed results while intake continues, and the same commands support handover and recovery.
- **Tests:** `env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v`, plus the spec’s individual `-k test_rNN_contract` filters; tests use temporary directories/databases, deterministic scripted responses and a blocked real network, so no test or build step needs a real API_KEY.
- **Model provider:** a provider interface with a scripted mock and a configurable OpenAI Responses adapter over an injected HTTPS JSON transport; request model ID, endpoint, request settings and timeout are explicit configuration, with production authentication read only from API_KEY and no credential stored in configuration fingerprints. Verify the exact supported request/response fields against current official provider documentation before implementation, record the chosen model ID/configuration in README and evidence, and test the real adapter entirely through intercepted transport rather than a live call.

The initial supported shared-operation arrangement is multiple CLI processes on one host using one local SQLite database; filesystem/network-share and multi-host database behavior are outside this arrangement and will be documented rather than claimed as tested. SQLite is the authoritative current/history store. Immutable attempts and source revisions are retained separately from current projections, with transactional current-record pointers. Extractions and queue views read the same committed attempt. Export both deliverables from one read snapshot into an immutable generation and expose the generation through one atomic directory reference, so a failed publication cannot expose a half-written generation; document the local-filesystem assumption. An operator reading multiple files across a publication switch must pin one generation. Interrupted workers are recovered through explicit resume with persisted work state and expiring claims; expired workers cannot overwrite a newer claim’s result. Bounded configurable worker concurrency, request timeouts and retry scheduling prevent one slow/rate-limited document from blocking unrelated work; exact tuning is documented as a limit, not a promised throughput.

Only successful, validated extraction results are reusable. Retry explicitly bypasses reuse for the selected document. Configuration identity includes producing provider/model/request settings, prompt and schema versions, and policy version; keep the actual nonsecret configuration alongside the identity. A policy-only change may reroute a retained valid extraction into a new attributed attempt; a failed current attempt is retried explicitly rather than silently replaced by historical success. An unchanged source byte hash distinguishes source identity from changes to producing settings. The latest accepted ingestion revision controls the current pointer; an older in-flight response can remain in history but cannot replace that revision. Order revisions by recorded ingestion sequence, since export timestamps are metadata and no cross-batch source ordering authority is specified.

Business-purpose prose and issue prose have no source-mandated exact wording. Fixtures record supported purpose facts and source quotes, while checking that the actual purpose expresses those facts without unsupported additions. The strict scalar metric compares the 11 non-purpose scalar fields, including nulls; purpose, issues and quote support receive separate checks/reports. This is a declared measurement choice, not a new application acceptance rule or a required accuracy score. The brief’s unspecified performance thresholds and issue vocabulary remain unspecified.

## Steps, in build order

Each numbered step starts by writing its owned tests and observing a failure for the intended missing behavior; collection errors, zero discovered tests and unexpected setup failures are not a meaningful red result. Implement just enough to make those tests pass, then run the complete mock suite. Each named test belongs to exactly one step; later steps may rerun it without taking ownership. Tests remain in `tests/test_spec_contract.py` with the spec’s method names unless a listed manual check is appropriate. Input fixtures and expected facts are authored independently of recorded model replies; the mock must never construct its replies by reading the oracle.

1. **Build the scripted mock provider first.** Spec lines: R-01 and R-102 are supported here; their final acceptance tests belong to steps 4 and 11.

   **Write first and observe red:** TP-01: `test_mock_provider_contract` and `test_mock_transport_contract`. Each test has its sole owner in this step and in Coverage.

   **Done when:** Create the provider contract and scripted mock in `intake/providers.py`, with an injected transport, saved response reading, call recording, barriers/delays, provider exceptions, refusal and incomplete-response events. Preserve `tests/test_starter.py` and its existing canned reply. Mock fixtures live in `tests/mock_responses/`; expected facts live separately in `tests/expected/`. The tests initially fail because the provider contract is missing, then demonstrate deterministic dispatch and no network/key dependency.

2. **Read exports and preserve independent document identity.** Spec lines: R-03, R-04, R-05, R-28, R-46

Report counts per field and case, exact numerator/denominator, unsupported facts, null/conflict/correction failures, purpose support and quote/issue checks separately. The mock script manifest must declare file-to-response scenarios, revision/settings variants and response_source; it is test/development configuration, never a business-fact extractor. #!/bin/bash
set -eu
ulimit -c 0
. /tmp/intake-step12-a11y.w1R0IS/environment
repo=/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests
work=$(mktemp -d "$trial/queue.XXXXXX")
export repo work
printf 'Queue evidence directory %s\n' "$work"
mkdir "$work/input" "$work/gates"
for name in IT-001 IT-002 IT-010; do cp "$repo/materials/requests/$name.json" "$work/input/"; done
printf '%s\n' '{"IT-001.json":["blocked-file.json"],"IT-002.json":["IT-002.json"],"IT-010.json":["provider-error.json"]}' > "$work/initial.json"

cat >"$work/pulse.conf" <<PULSE
load-module module-native-protocol-unix socket=$work/pulse.sock auth-anonymous=1
load-module module-null-sink sink_name=intake_audit
set-default-sink intake_audit
PULSE
export PULSE_SERVER="unix:$work/pulse.sock"
pulse_modules=$(dirname "$(find "$root_trial/usr/lib" -name module-null-sink.so -print -quit)")
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH="$LD_LIBRARY_PATH:$pulse_modules:$root_trial/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/pulseaudio"
pulseaudio --daemonize=no --exit-idle-time=-1 --disable-shm=yes --dl-search-path="$pulse_modules" \
    --use-pid-file=no --log-target=stderr -n -F "$work/pulse.conf" >"$work/pulse.log" 2>&1 &
pulse_pid=$!
trap 'kill "$pulse_pid" 2>/dev/null || true' EXIT
for i in {1..45}; do
    if pactl info >"$work/pulse-info.txt" 2>/dev/null; then break; fi
    sleep .1
done
pactl list short sinks || { cat "$work/pulse.log"; exit 1; }
parecord --device=intake_audit.monitor --file-format=wav "$work/speech.wav" >"$work/parecord.log" 2>&1 &
record_pid=$!
source <(sed -n '4,/^speech_pid=/{p;}' "$trial/probe.sh")
trap 'for pid in ${terminal_pid:-} ${orca_pid:-} ${speech_pid:-} ${wm_pid:-} ${registry_pid:-} ${bus_pid:-} ${worker_pid:-} "$x_pid" "$record_pid" "$pulse_pid"; do kill "$pid" 2>/dev/null || true; done' EXIT
orca --debug --debug-file "$work/orca.log" --enable=speech >"$work/orca-stderr.log" 2>&1 &
orca_pid=$!
sleep 1
cd "$repo"
.venv/bin/python -m intake run --input "$work/input" --db "$work/intake.db" --provider mock \
    --responses tests/mock_responses --script "$work/initial.json" --mock-gates "$work/gates" --timeout 150 \
    >"$work/intake.log" 2>&1 &
worker_pid=$!
for i in {1..80}; do
    if test -e "$work/gates/entered" &&
        .venv/bin/python -m intake queue --db "$work/intake.db" --include-pending --format text >"$work/wait.txt" &&
        rg -q 'Next action: retry-extraction' "$work/wait.txt" && rg -q 'Owner: Security Review' "$work/wait.txt"; then break; fi
    sleep .1
done

cat >"$work/bashrc" <<'RC'
PS1='queue-test$ '
cd "$repo"
show_queue() {
    "$repo/.venv/bin/python" -m intake queue --db "$work/intake.db" --include-pending --format text >"$work/queue.txt"
    LESS= less -j1 "$work/queue.txt"
}
RC
xfce4-terminal --disable-server --font='DejaVu Sans Mono 12' --geometry=126x42 --title='Orca Queue' \
    --command="/bin/bash --rcfile $work/bashrc -i" >"$work/terminal.log" 2>&1 &
terminal_pid=$!
window=$(timeout 10 xdotool search --sync --onlyvisible --name 'Orca Queue' | head -n 1)
test -n "$window"
timeout 8 xdotool windowactivate --sync "$window"
xdotool type --clearmodifiers --delay 25 show_queue
xdotool key Return
for i in {1..55}; do
    if test -s "$work/queue.txt"; then break; fi
    sleep .1
done
sleep 1
for document in IT-001 IT-002 IT-010; do
    xdotool key --clearmodifiers g
    if [[ "$document" != IT-001 ]]; then
        xdotool key --clearmodifiers slash
        xdotool type --clearmodifiers "Document: $document"
        xdotool key Return
    fi
    sleep 1
    wc -l < "$work/orca.log" > "$work/$document-nav-start.txt"
    xdotool key --clearmodifiers Insert+KP_Home
    sleep 1.5
    for i in {1..9}; do
        xdotool key --clearmodifiers KP_Prior
        sleep 1.2
    done
    xdotool key --clearmodifiers KP_Subtract
    sleep .5
    wc -l < "$work/orca.log" > "$work/$document-nav-end.txt"
done
xdotool key --clearmodifiers q
sleep 1
for document in IT-001 IT-002 IT-010; do
    start=$(cat "$work/$document-nav-start.txt")
    end=$(cat "$work/$document-nav-end.txt")
    printf '\n%s Orca review\n' "$document"
    sed -n "$((start+1)),${end}p" "$work/orca.log" | rg "SPEECH DISPATCHER: Speaking '[[:space:]]*(Document|Work state|Owner|Status|Next action|Error|Retry command)"
done

+Reuse applies to successful, validated results. Retry explicitly bypasses reuse for the selected document. Configuration identity includes producing provider/model/request settings, prompt and schema versions, and policy version; keep the actual nonsecret configuration alongside the identity. A policy change triggers re-extraction and routing under a new attributed attempt. Explicit retry records a new attempt and leaves historical success available in history. An unchanged source byte hash distinguishes source identity from changes to producing settings. The latest accepted ingestion revision controls the current pointer; an older in-flight response can remain in history but cannot replace that revision. Order revisions by recorded ingestion sequence, since export timestamps are metadata and no cross-batch source ordering authority is specified.

# Northstar access-request intake

A Python CLI turns exported free-text messages into schema-validated extraction records and an ordered human-review queue. It prepares requests for people; a named manager is a contact, and successful intake never means approval.

## Setup and tests

Supported environment: Python 3.11+ on a local POSIX filesystem; this submission was exercised with Python 3.12 on Linux. Install `uv`, then run from the repository root:

```bash
uv sync --frozen
. .venv/bin/activate
env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

`pyproject.toml` declares jsonschema; `uv.lock` locks it and its dependencies. Setup may download locked packages. Tests and mock intake need no credentials or network. The tests forbid sockets and any read of API_KEY, including in guarded CLI subprocesses. A real-provider authentication unit check injects an inert credential function and inspects the environment-reader source; it never calls that reader. Target one planned test with `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -k test_r53_contract -v`; zero discovered tests is not a pass.

## Reproducible mock intake and inspection

These commands run after activation from the repository root. Use a fresh database path for a fresh demonstration; rerunning the same input/configuration reuses completed valid work.

<!-- smoke -->
```bash
python3 -m intake run --input materials/requests --db var/demo.sqlite --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses --output deliverables
python3 -m intake queue --db var/demo.sqlite --include-pending
python3 -m intake resume --db var/demo.sqlite --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses
python3 -m intake retry --db var/demo.sqlite --document IT-010.json --provider mock --responses tests/mock_responses
python3 -m intake history --db var/demo.sqlite --document IT-010.json
python3 -m intake export --db var/demo.sqlite --output deliverables
```

`run` accepts a directory or one exported JSON file. `queue` reads committed current outcomes even while another CLI process is preparing other documents; `--include-pending` also shows pending/running work without pretending it has a completed business status. `history` retains every attempt with its source bytes/hash, configuration, policy identity and outcome. Inputs absent from a later batch remain present. A corrected message or relevant producing-settings change creates a new attempt; `--refresh` explicitly forces one. Explicit retry bypasses reuse, and a failed retry becomes the current error while previous success remains identifiable in history.
"""Publish matching queue and extraction files through one atomic generation pointer."""
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path
import uuid

QUEUE_FIELDS = ['document_id', 'source_sha256', 'attempt_id', 'source_revision', 'status', 'owner', 'next_action', 'error']


def write_synced(path, text):
    with path.open('w', encoding='utf-8') as stream:
        stream.write(text)
        stream.flush()
        os.fsync(stream.fileno())


def sync_directory(path):
    descriptor = os.open(path, os.O_RDONLY | os.O_DIRECTORY)
    try:
        os.fsync(descriptor)
    finally:
        os.close(descriptor)


def _publish(store, output, hook=None):
    hook = hook or (lambda stage: None)
    output = Path(output)
    output.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    generations = output / '.generations'
    generations.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    name = uuid.uuid4().hex
    generation = generations / name
    generation.mkdir()
    # One SELECT snapshot provides the input for both files.
    records = store.current()
    write_synced(generation / 'extractions.jsonl', ''.join(json.dumps(row, sort_keys=True) + '\n' for row in records))
    hook('after-extractions')
    queue = [{key: row.get(key) for key in QUEUE_FIELDS} for row in records]
    write_synced(generation / 'queue.json', json.dumps(queue, indent=2, sort_keys=True) + '\n')
    hook('after-queue')
    sync_directory(generation)
    sync_directory(generations)
    # These stable links always traverse the same directory pointer. Readers pin
    # `current.resolve()` before reading multiple files across concurrent publication.
    for filename in ['extractions.jsonl', 'queue.json']:
        public = output / filename
        if not public.is_symlink():
            temporary = output / f'.{filename}-{name}'
            temporary.symlink_to(f'current/{filename}')
            os.replace(temporary, public)
    pointer = output / f'.current-{name}'
    pointer.symlink_to(f'.generations/{name}', target_is_directory=True)
    hook('before-publish')
    os.replace(pointer, output / 'current')
    sync_directory(output)
    hook('after-publish')
    return generation


def publish(store, output, hook=None):
    import fcntl
    output = Path(output)
    output.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    # Hold the local-host advisory lock from snapshot acquisition through pointer
    # replacement, preventing a slow old publisher from overwriting a newer one.
    with (output / '.publish.lock').open('a') as lock:
        fcntl.flock(lock.fileno(), fcntl.LOCK_EX)
        try:
            return _publish(store, output, hook)
        finally:
            fcntl.flock(lock.fileno(), fcntl.LOCK_UN)

All 115 automated tests passed, but the accessibility replay can race with worker completion, the tested HTML presentation cannot be reproduced from the documented steps, and the new pager workflow leaves a plaintext queue export behind.

Full review comments:

- [P2] Wait for all three queue states before interrupting intake — /home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/planning/plan.md:206-209
  The `entered` marker only confirms that IT-001 reached its gate; it does not mean IT-002 and IT-010 have committed their results. In 30 local replays, a snapshot taken as soon as the marker appeared still showed at least one of those requests unfinished. If the operator terminates intake then, the replay cannot verify that resume preserved IT-002’s committed result. Repeat the queue check until IT-001 is running, IT-002 is completed, and IT-010 is failed before sending `SIGTERM`.

- [P2] Page live queue output without writing a plaintext copy — /home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/README.md:55-56
  When operators substitute a live database for the demo, this redirection leaves requester names, access details, and source excerpts in `queue.txt`. With a common `022` umask the file is created with mode `0644`, and it remains after `less` exits. Pipe the output directly to `less -j1` so operators can search and review it without leaving an untracked copy.

- [P2] Make the tested HTML rendering reproducible — /home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/deliverables/verification.md:134-134
  The Firefox results depend on a custom HTML wrapper and link handling that the documented Markdown extensions do not provide. For example, the README targets `verification.md`, and Python-Markdown does not rewrite that link to the local HTML report. A reviewer following the replay cannot recreate the presentation used to verify the landmark, focus style, and cross-document navigation required by [R-111 and R-114](../planning/spec.md#L128-L131). Include the rendering command or script, with its wrapper and link mapping.

- [P3] Announce text-mode progress before reading exports — /home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/intake/__main__.py:158-160
  Text mode previously flushed its startup message before reading the exports. It now stays silent until every file has been read and parsed, so a large batch or slow filesystem can leave a screen-reader user without any indication that intake has started. Emit a labelled reading-progress message before the loop while keeping the new filename-specific errors.

# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.
# Block 3. Implement, then validate against the spec

Codex now builds from your plan, one step at a time, each test written before the code it tests and
run on mock responses. Then you **validate**: you check what was built against the spec, line by
line, and mark each line met or not met, with evidence you can open or run again. Validation is
yours, not the agent's. Codex's summary of what it did is a claim about the code, not evidence: an
agent can report a step done that its tests never exercise.

Start from your committed `planning/plan.md` (`docs/02-plan-with-test-plan.md`).

## Part 1. Build, test first, on mock responses

1. Start Codex in the root of your clone and ask it to build `planning/plan.md` in its step order.
   Your request says:
   - for each step, first write the test the plan names, run it and show it failing, then stop;
     after you commit the failing test (`Test first: <step>`), write the code until it passes, then
     stop again so you commit it (`Step <n>: <step>`);
   - every test uses mock responses saved under `tests/mock_responses/`, and no test calls the real
     model or reads `API_KEY`;
   - the expected values in each test are the expected facts of the test plan, not values copied
     from a run;
   - after each step, run the whole test suite and stop if anything fails.
2. You make the commits: Codex's sandbox does not let it write to `.git`, and the commits are your
   record that each test failed before its code existed. If a step's new test already passes
   before any code is written, say so in its commit message (`Test first: <step> (already
   passes)`) rather than making it fail on purpose.
3. Watch the steps. After each one, run the tests yourself, with `API_KEY` unset:

   ```bash
   env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests
   ```

   (If your plan chose another test command, use it, still with `API_KEY` unset, and write it in
   your README.)
4. When the steps are done, save the full test run and commit it with anything not yet committed:

   ```bash
   env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v > planning/test-run.txt 2>&1
   git add -A
   git commit -m "Build the plan's steps, tests first, on mock responses"
   ```

## Part 2. Validate each spec line

1. Create `planning/validation.md` with one row per line of `planning/spec.md`:

   | Spec line | Requirement | Met or not met | Evidence | Note |
   |---|---|---|---|---|

2. Fill each row yourself. You may ask Codex to point you to code or tests, but you open the
   evidence and you decide the mark:
   - **Evidence** is something a reviewer can open or run again: a test name and its line in
     `planning/test-run.txt`, a file and line in the code, or a command and what it printed.
   - A line is **met** only when its evidence shows the requirement. A test that passes but does not
     test this requirement is not evidence for it.
   - A line with no evidence, or evidence for only part of it, is **not met**, and the note says what
     is missing.
3. Under the table, write the count: how many lines are met, how many are not met.
4. Commit:

   ```bash
   git add planning/validation.md
   git commit -m "Validation: each spec line met or not met, with evidence"
   ```

## What is on disk at the end

- The code and its tests, the tests passing on mock responses.
- `planning/test-run.txt`: the saved run.
- `planning/validation.md`: every spec line marked met or not met, each with its evidence.

## How to tell it is right

- `planning/validation.md` has as many rows as `planning/spec.md`.
- Pick two rows marked met and open their evidence: each shows the requirement, not only a passing test.
- `env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` ends with `OK` on a fresh run.
- `git log --oneline` shows a `Test first:` commit before each step's code commit.

## After class, on your own

1. The spec lines marked not met: plan each, build it test first, and mark it again.
2. The review queue: run intake on the 20 exports and check each entry's status, owner and next
   action against the five rules of `materials/office-policy.md`, in order.
3. The accuracy check: compare the extracted fields with the expected facts you wrote from the
   messages, as `CHALLENGE.md` asks for `deliverables/accuracy.md`.
4. The rest of the files `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit lists under `deliverables/`, and the README
   it asks for. Class time covers the spec, the plan, the build and its validation; these files
   finish the submission.

Run recovery with `resume` after a crash or deployment interruption. It continues pending work and running work whose claim expired; the default claim lifetime is request timeout + 5 seconds. An active claim is left alone. Resume reconstructs settings per document, supports parallel progress and refreshes work if prompt/schema/policy versions changed. An older or expired worker token cannot replace a newer claim's result. Pending work with changed settings is marked superseded in history rather than mislabelled as produced under those earlier settings.

Each error includes an actionable diagnostic and a reproducible `retry_command`; use that command against the same recorded database/configuration. CLI exit status is 0 on successful execution, 1 when current error records or failed accuracy comparisons remain, and 2 for command/input/configuration errors. A `needs-information` request is successful intake awaiting clarification, not an extraction error.

## Keyboard and screen-reader operation

Add `--format text` after any subcommand for labelled output in reading order. This mode uses ordinary terminal text with no color, animation, cursor control or timed input. Each queue entry starts with its document name and work state, followed by its routing, errors and retry guidance when available. In history, each attempt has its own state, source and producing settings. Use the terminal's screen-reader navigation commands to review earlier lines. Font size, contrast and cursor preferences are set in the terminal.

```bash

python3 -m intake queue --help
python3 -m intake queue --db var/demo.sqlite --include-pending --format text
python3 -m intake history --db var/demo.sqlite --document IT-010.json --format text
```

Use the same `--format text` option with `run`, `resume`, `retry`, `export` and `accuracy`. While intake or resume is active, inspect progress from a second terminal with `queue --include-pending`. Read the `Retry command` line under the failed document and run it to retry that document. `export --format text` identifies the published generation, and `accuracy --format text` gives the match count and report path. JSON remains the default for command output and the format of the machine-readable exports.

Use a keyboard-operable terminal exposing its text through the platform's accessibility services, such as Xfce Terminal with Orca on Linux. See the [Section 508 verification results](deliverables/verification.md#section-508-accessibility) for tested versions, workflows and scope.

Mock mode reads only saved JSON replies and the development manifest under `tests/mock_responses/`; it never reads API_KEY. `--script` selects another saved manifest. The production extractor does not look up known filenames or import tests/expected. `--mock-gates` is a development-only directory of file barriers for repeatable process/interruption tests.
